items.text:
You may not know all the answers yet. “I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out with you” is a perfectly good answer.

And what is sex for each of you? One of you may mainly think of it as bonding, and for the other it’s more like play. Sometimes it may feel sacred; another time it may just be how you come down from a bad day. Sex doesn’t have to mean the same thing every time, as long as you can tell each other what it means to you.

It’s important to talk about sexual compatibility before getting undressed, even if that kills the vibe. Or even especially if it does kill the vibe, actually, since that’s a red flag if talking ruins things. And this applies whether you’re leaning too libertine or too traditional. And once you are undressed, the communication doesn’t stop there either. Can you feel comfortable with each other enough to express what turns you on, what this means to you, and what you’re unsure about? It’s that psychological trust & intimacy that builds the bridge between “having sex” and “making love.”

I remember reading a Christian magazine’s letter from a newlywed Christian woman who found out that her husband didn’t have much interest in sex after she saved herself for marriage. He trapped her, because he knew she would not feel good about divorce due to the religion. Of course, it didn’t have to be nefarious. I had a relationship with E. that was a bit like that about 15yrs ago. She wanted sex once a week, and it was driving me nuts because my libido was thru the roof. She also had no interest in trying to take a safe herb or supplement to increase her desire. Of course everyone does change over time as well, so if our libidos diverge later, let’s talk about what we’d do before either of us is already hurt.
